name: EBWF World Heavy Weight Championship
epitaph: Kurt Angle won it vacant on 15 April 2002, the earliest date the promotion's own record carries, and it changed hands forty-eight times across six years. Raven took it nine times between June 2002 and April 2004, more often than anyone else; Christian took it seven times, once in 2002 and six more across 2005 and 2006. It emptied four times — in June 2002, after the King of the Ring in June 2004, in November 2005, and on 1 September 2006, the day after Chris Jericho won it, when his own retirement ended a reign one day old. Triple H's win at Wrestlemania 7 on 30 March 2008 is the last change recorded, and the promotion's own Champions page still names him champion.

name: EBWF Women's Championship
epitaph: Molly Holly held it first, from 15 April 2002. Torrie Wilson took it eight times over four years, Lita and Stacy Keibler five each, across fifty-two reigns. Lita's last ended without a match: the Title History records her retiring with the belt at Backlash on 30 April 2006 and giving it to Kristal, who is listed as champion from that December. The reign before hers ended in the one vacancy the page explains by a handler leaving the promotion. Jillian Hall's win at Aftermath on 27 April 2008 is the last change recorded, and the promotion's own Champions page still names her champion.

name: EBWF Tag Team Championships
epitaph: The Hulkamaniacs — The Undertaker and Hulk Hogan — held it first, from 15 April 2002, lost it at Backlash that month and took it back a week later. Team 3:16, The Rock and Stone Cold Steve Austin, took it three times in 2002 alone. Six of its forty-five reigns changed hands on storyline rather than in a match: four between August 2005 and March 2006, as injuries and a retirement moved half the championship between Shannon Moore, Wes Ikeda, Jeff Hardy and Scotty 2 Hotty, and two more in 2007, when Syxx and then Jeff Hardy vacated their own halves and the other holder kept his. D-Generation X's win at Death Before Dishonor on 25 May 2008 is the last change the whole Title History records, of any EBWF belt.
notes: Source: the promotion's own Title History page (/promotions/ebwf-2001/archive/titlehistory.html). Two reigns are printed with one name on both sides (“Raven & Raven”, 14 December 2003; “Bret Hart & Bret Hart”, 25 May 2003); they are recorded as printed.

name: EBWF Intercontinental Championship
epitaph: HHH opened it on 11 April 2002 and held it five separate times through December 2002, more than anyone else took it. Vampiro's four reigns run from November 2004 to February 2007, the last of them won in a tournament after the belt had been vacated. Christian took it three times and Randy Orton three, and Bret Hart held it twice in 2003. The Miz's win at Death Before Dishonor on 25 May 2008 closes its own record, and the promotion's own Champions page still names him champion.

name: EBWF Hardcore Championship
epitaph: Tommy Dreamer held it first, from 15 April 2002, and took it three times in its opening year. Fifty-seven reigns ran through it in four and a half years, faster than any other EBWF belt changed hands: The Hurricane took it four times across 2004 and 2005, Cactus Jack, Chris Benoit and David Flair three each. At the Destiny Pay-Per-View on 24 September 2006 the promotion renamed it the No Limits Championship, with Raven's own reign running through the change and on into the new name's record.

events.title: ebwf-2001-no-limits
events.note: The Title History's own entry: “Hardcore Title renamed No Limit Championship - PPV: Destiny - Sunday, September 24, 2006”.

notes: Source: the promotion's own Title History page (/promotions/ebwf-2001/archive/titlehistory.html). The Title History carries this lineage under the No Limits name, which it writes as “Hardcore Title” only in the rename entry itself; no page read gives the belt a longer name than that.

name: EBWF No Limits Championship
epitaph: The Hardcore Championship's own lineage under a new name, renamed at the Destiny Pay-Per-View on 24 September 2006 with Raven still holding it. Raven's reign ran on until the belt was emptied over his own inactive status, and Sting won it from the vacancy in a battle royal at Aftermath on 29 April 2007. Triple H took it from him at Death Before Dishonor that July and it was vacated again on Warfare on 15 October 2007. Lacey's win at Survivor Series on 25 November 2007 is the last change recorded, and the promotion's own Champions page still names her champion.

name: EBWF LHW Championship
epitaph: Christian held it first, from 15 April 2002, and Lita took it from him that May — the one reign a woman holds on this belt's record. Rey Mysterio Jr. and The Hurricane traded it through 2003, three reigns to four, and it was emptied twice in 2002, at Unforgiven that September and on Smackdown that November. At the Destiny Pay-Per-View on 24 September 2006 the promotion renamed it the X-Division Championship, with Syxx's own reign running through the change and on into the new name's record.

events.title: ebwf-2001-x-division
events.note: The Title History's own entry: “LHW Title renamed X-Divsion Championship - PPV: Destiny - Sunday, September 24, 2006”.

notes: Source: the promotion's own Title History page (/promotions/ebwf-2001/archive/titlehistory.html). The Title History writes this belt's own name only as “LHW Title”, in the rename entry, and no page read spells the abbreviation out.

name: EBWF X-Division Championship
epitaph: The LHW Championship's own lineage under a new name, renamed at the Destiny Pay-Per-View on 24 September 2006 with Syxx still holding it. Thirteen reigns follow in under two years, seven of them inside 2008 alone — one of those won by Val Venis at a house show on 8 January, two days after the belt had been vacated at another. Ron Killings and Paul London took it twice each that spring. Rob Van Dam's win at Death Before Dishonor on 25 May 2008 is the last change recorded, and the promotion's own Champions page still names him champion.

name: EBWF European Championship
epitaph: The Title History opens this belt with “Started W/The Rock” on Smackdown, 18 March 2004 — the same night it retires the Multicontinental US Championship with The Rock holding that one too. Twenty-three reigns follow in two and a half years: Mark Jindrak, Booker T, Ric Flair, Petey Williams, Shane Helms and Kane each take it twice. At the Destiny Pay-Per-View on 24 September 2006 the promotion renamed it the Iron Man Championship, on the same night Kane won it, and his reign carries into the new name's record.

events.title: ebwf-2001-iron-man
events.note: The Title History's own entry: “European Title renamed Iron Man Championship - PPV: Destiny - Sunday, September 24, 2006”, printed directly above Kane's own win at the same card.

notes: Source: the promotion's own Title History page (/promotions/ebwf-2001/archive/titlehistory.html). The Title History writes this belt's own name only as “European Title”, in the rename entry. Whether the Multicontinental US lineage passed into this belt on 18 March 2004, or simply ended as this one began, is not stated anywhere read.

name: EBWF Iron Man Championship
epitaph: The European Championship's own lineage under a new name, renamed at the Destiny Pay-Per-View on 24 September 2006, the night Kane won it. Triple H took it from him on Aggression that October, and lost it at Survivor Series on 26 November 2006 without wrestling for it: the Title History records Rene Dupree beating Shawn Michaels, who was defending the title on Triple H's behalf. Dupree held it for the rest of its run, until the belt was retired on Aggression on 1 November 2007.

events.note: The Title History's own entry: “Belt Retired - Aggression - Thursday, November 1, 2007”, the same night it retires the Television Championship.

name: EBWF People's Championship
epitaph: Kane held it first, from 15 April 2002. John Cena took it five times between 2003 and 2005 and Booker T four in 2002 and 2003; Kurt Angle and Chris Jericho — billed on this belt's record as Y2J Chris Jericho — traded it five times between them across the winter of 2004. Two of its forty-nine reigns began on the same night, 4 October 2004, when Christian and then The Undertaker each held it, and The Undertaker's own retirement emptied it two days later. At the Destiny Pay-Per-View on 24 September 2006 the promotion renamed it the Television Championship, with Alex Shelley's own reign running through the change.

events.title: ebwf-2001-television
events.note: The Title History's own entry: “People's Title renamed Television Championship - PPV: Destiny - Sunday, September 24, 2006”.

notes: Source: the promotion's own Title History page (/promotions/ebwf-2001/archive/titlehistory.html). The Title History writes this belt's own name only as “People's Title”, in the rename entry.

name: EBWF Television Championship
epitaph: The People's Championship's own lineage under a new name, renamed at the Destiny Pay-Per-View on 24 September 2006 while Alex Shelley held it. Randy Orton took it from him at the King of the Ring in June 2007 and Lance Storm took it at Destiny that September. Storm held it until the belt was retired on Aggression on 1 November 2007, the same night as the Iron Man Championship.

events.note: The Title History's own entry: “Belt Retired - Aggression - Thursday, November 1, 2007”.

name: EBWF Multicontinental US Championship
epitaph: The Rock held it first, from 11 April 2002, and last: he took it a third time at Wrestlemania on 14 March 2004 and the Title History retires the belt with him four nights later, on the same Smackdown it opens the European Championship with him. Twenty-one reigns run between: Stone Cold Steve Austin took it three times in 2002 and 2003, Bret Hart and Christian twice each. It is one of three EBWF belts whose whole record ends before the promotion did.

events.note: The Title History's own entry: “Retired W/The Rock - Smackdown - Thursday, March 18, 2004” — the same entry date on which it opens the European Championship with “Started W/The Rock”.

notes: Source: the promotion's own Title History page (/promotions/ebwf-2001/archive/titlehistory.html). Two stretches of this belt's own history are printed out of their own date order (August 2002 and June 2003); the rows follow the dates the page itself gives. Its August 2002 entries place two Christian reigns back to back with no loss between them, which the page does not resolve.
